---
title: "How to load channel features"
---

This guide downloads and loads the **channel-level ephys feature aggregates** — the core
dataset of the IBL Ephys Atlas. Each row is one recording channel from one probe
insertion, annotated with its brain region and its electrophysiological features.

::: {.callout-important}
## This needs an IBL account

These aggregates live in a private S3 bucket, and authentication goes through
`one.api.ONE` with Alyx credentials. Pass a logged-in `ONE` instance as the `one`
argument to every download function.

If you have no IBL account, you can still
[compute features from your own recording](compute-features-spikeglx.qmd) and
[run the published models](download-models.qmd) — both work without credentials.
:::

## S3 layout

```text
aggregates/atlas/features/{project}/{label}/agg_full/
├── raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt   denoised per-channel features  (~175 MB)
├── raw_ephys_features.pqt            raw per-channel features       (~165 MB)
├── channels.pqt                      channel metadata (coordinates, probe info)  (~10 MB)
├── df_all_cols_merged.pqt            denoised + channels + region ids, pre-merged (~185 MB)
└── snippets_df.pqt                   per-snippet provenance manifest
```

Features are versioned with a weekly `YYYY_Www` label — a **vintage**. See the
[S3 layout reference](../reference/s3-layout.qmd) for the full tree and for how this
file list changed across vintages (`channels_labels.pqt` is legacy; channel labels are now
a `labels` column inside `channels.pqt`).

## Download

```python
from pathlib import Path

from one.api import ONE
import ephysatlas.data

one = ONE(base_url="https://alyx.internationalbrainlab.org", mode="remote")
local_path = Path("/datadisk/ephys-atlas/features")
label = "2026_W42"

# downloads to local_path/ea_active/{label}/agg_full/
path_features = ephysatlas.data.download_tables(local_path, label=label, one=one)
```

Pass `extended=True` to also fetch the `{label}_extended/` folder, which holds large
optional datasets such as cross-correlograms:

```python
ephysatlas.data.download_tables(local_path, label=label, one=one, extended=True)
```

## Load

```python
import ephysatlas.data
import ephysatlas.anatomy

brain_atlas = ephysatlas.anatomy.ClassifierAtlas()
df_features = ephysatlas.data.read_features_from_disk(
    path_features, brain_atlas=brain_atlas
)
```

`read_features_from_disk` merges the denoised features with `channels.pqt` into one
DataFrame indexed by `(pid, channel)`, and annotates every channel with `Allen_id`,
`Cosmos_id` and `Beryl_id` region ids. Channel quality labels come from the `labels` column
inside `channels.pqt`, falling back to a separate `channels_labels.pqt` on older vintages.

Two things happen on the way:

- **Validation picks the schema from the columns present.** A table with the spike-shape
  columns (`spike_width_secs`, ..., denoised tables from `2026_W39` on) is checked
  against `ModelDenoisedFeatures`. A table with the raw waveform columns (the raw table,
  and older denoised tables) is checked against `ModelRawFeatures`.
- **The alpha features get an outlier treatment.** Values at or above 1000 times their
  column's median are replaced by the median. It applies to the first column group the
  table carries: `alpha_mean` / `alpha_std`, else `psd_alpha` / `psd_alpha_csd` (an
  LF-only table), else either of those alone
  (`ephysatlas.data.alpha_outlier_columns`).

Useful arguments:

| argument | default | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `brain_atlas` | `ClassifierAtlas()` | The atlas used to map coordinates to regions |
| `mappings` | `["Cosmos", "Beryl"]` | Which region ontologies to add as `{mapping}_id` columns |
| `load_denoised` | `True` | Read the denoised table; `False` reads `raw_ephys_features.pqt` |
| `strict` | `True` | Validate against the pandera schema; `False` skips the validation |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Skip it entirely on recent vintages

The default `brain_atlas=ClassifierAtlas()` downloads the Allen template volumes on first
use — hundreds of megabytes.

From `2025_W39` on you rarely need it: `df_all_cols_merged.pqt` **is** the output of
`read_features_from_disk`, already merged and region-annotated.

```python
import pandas as pd

df_features = pd.read_parquet(path_features / "df_all_cols_merged.pqt")
# 70 columns: 53 denoised features + channel metadata
#             + Allen_id / Cosmos_id / Beryl_id / outside
```

No atlas download, no merge, no schema validation pass. Use `read_features_from_disk` when
you need `load_denoised=False`, a non-default `mappings` list, or an older vintage.
:::

The denoised table stores `rms_ap` / `rms_lf` in dB and `spike_count` in log2 (from
vintage `2025_W28` on). Set `load_denoised=False` for the untransformed values. From
`2026_W39` on, the tables are computed with `ephysatlas` 0.9.0: waveform amplitudes are
in volts, `spike_count` is a rate in spikes/s, and the denoised table carries the
spike-shape columns instead of the six raw waveform columns. The raw table keeps the
raw ones. From `2026_W42` the first-difference CSD columns are `*_bpr`, Cadzow-denoised
with the ibl-neuropixel 1.14 defaults, and `read_features_from_disk` renames the
`*_csd_diff1` columns of older tables to match. See the
[feature list](../reference/feature-list.qmd).

## Find the available vintages

```python
labels = ephysatlas.data.list_available_labels(one=one, project="ea_active")
print(labels[:5])   # newest first: ['2026_W42', '2026_W39', '2026_W38', '2026_W37', '2026_W32']

latest = ephysatlas.data.get_latest_label(one=one, project="ea_active")   # '2026_W42'

projects = ephysatlas.data.list_available_projects(one=one)
```

Two projects exist:

- **`ea_active`** — the default, updated weekly with the latest features
- **`ibl_neuropixel_brainwide_01`** — the frozen brainwide-map dataset

::: {.callout-tip}
Pin an explicit `label` in any analysis you intend to reproduce. `get_latest_label`
resolves to whatever is newest *today*, which is convenient and not reproducible — and if
you then run a published model over it, the model's vintage and the feature vintage must
still match. The newest features can be newer than any model. As of October 2026 the
latest label is `2026_W42`, and so are the newest models, so these pages use `2026_W42`.
:::
